items.stem: Briefly explain why a sample, rather than a census, is usually used in statistical investigations.
items.answer: A census is often too expensive, slow or impossible (e.g. destructive testing); a well-chosen sample gives reliable information about the population at much lower cost.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A census is often too expensive, slow or impossible (e.g. destructive testing); a well-chosen sample gives reliable information about the population at much lower cost. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Isabel writes: "A large sample is always representative of the population." Explain why this is inaccurate.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "continuous data"?
options: The square of the standard deviation
Data that can take any value in an interval, usually measurements
Checking reliability by giving two equivalent versions of a test to the same group and correlating the results
The middle value of the ordered data (mean of the two middle values when n is even)
items.answer: Data that can take any value in an interval, usually measurements
items.markingKey: B. "continuous data" is data that can take any value in an interval, usually measurements.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "standard deviation"?
options: A list of all members of the population from which a sample can be drawn
Checking reliability by giving the same test to the same group on two occasions and correlating the results
A measure of spread: the square root of the mean of the squared deviations from the mean (σ on the GDC)
The extent to which a measurement or survey gives consistent results when repeated under the same conditions
items.answer: A measure of spread: the square root of the mean of the squared deviations from the mean (σ on the GDC)
items.markingKey: C. "standard deviation" is a measure of spread: the square root of the mean of the squared deviations from the mean (σ on the GDC).

items.stem: Briefly explain why the standard deviation is more affected by an outlier than the interquartile range.
items.answer: σ uses every value and squares the deviations, so one extreme value adds a large squared term; the IQR depends only on the quartiles.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: σ uses every value and squares the deviations, so one extreme value adds a large squared term; the IQR depends only on the quartiles. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A data set has mean 23.3 and standard deviation 14.4. Each value is transformed by y = 0.5x + 1. Find the new mean and standard deviation, explaining why the constant 1 affects only one of them.

items.stem: In a mathematics test, class A (21 students) had a mean score of 65.9 and class B (30 students) had a mean of 54.5. (a) Find the mean score of all 51 students. items.answer: (a) 59.2 (b) 122 (c) classes differ in size (d) mean +5, sd unchanged
items.markingKey: (a) (21 × 65.9 + 30 × 54.5)/51 (M1) = 59.2 (A1). (b) 60.4 × 52 − 3018.9 (M1) = 122 (A1). (c) R1 weighted by class size. (d) A1 mean increases by 5; A1 sd unchanged.

items.stem: 8 people take a reaction-time app twice, one month apart. Their scores (first, second) are: (69, 66); (63, 62); (58, 58); (47, 47); (46, 48); (54, 56); (93, 90); (80, 79). Calculate Pearson's r and state what kind of reliability is being tested.
items.markingKey: GDC (M1); r = 0.997 (A1); test-retest (A1).

items.stem: "Online surveys are the best way to collect data about the reading habits of teenagers." Discuss.
items.answer: Online surveys are convenient but likely biased; combining them with a stratified sample in schools would improve validity.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: cheap, fast and reach many teenagers; anonymity may encourage honest answers. Arguments against: self-selection bias: keen readers more likely to respond; excludes those without internet access; cannot check who answers. Supported judgement: Online surveys are convenient but likely biased; combining them with a stratified sample in schools would improve validity. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Every value in a data set is multiplied by 3. What happens to the variance?
items.markingKey: C. σ is multiplied by 3, so σ² by 9.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A subset of the population from which data are collected"?
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of sample.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "modal class"?
options: Data that can take any value in an interval, usually measurements
The square of the standard deviation
The class with the highest frequency
A bar chart of grouped continuous data with no gaps between bars, bar heights showing frequency for equal class widths
items.answer: The class with the highest frequency
items.markingKey: C. "modal class" is the class with the highest frequency.

items.stem: To check an anxiety questionnaire, a researcher gives it to 8 people and repeats it a week later; Pearson's r between the two sets of scores is 0.996. Explain what this suggests about the reliability of the test.
items.markingKey: R1 this is a test-retest check of reliability; R1 r = 0.996 indicates a strong positive correlation, so the test gives consistent results.

items.stem: A data set has mean 31.9 and standard deviation 11.7. Each value is transformed by y = 3x + 2. Find the new mean and standard deviation, explaining why the constant 2 affects only one of them.
items.markingKey: new mean = 3 × 31.9 + 2 = 97.6 (A1); new sd = 3 × 11.7 = 35.1 (A1); R1 adding 2 shifts all values and the mean equally, leaving deviations unchanged.

items.stem: From an alphabetical list of 1074 students, a starting point is chosen at random and then every 22th student is selected. Identify the sampling technique and explain one disadvantage of using it here.
items.markingKey: A1 systematic sampling; R1 it can be biased if there is a pattern in the list that matches the interval; R1 linked to this context.

items.stem: A head teacher wants to survey students about a new timetable. The school has 124 students in Year 12, 172 students in Year 9, 186 students in Year 11, 185 students in Year 10. items.markingKey: (a) R1 opinions may differ between year groups, so each should be represented in proportion. (b) M1 A2 (14.9, 20.6, 22.3, 22.2). (c) R1 simple random sampling from a list of each year group. (d) R1 non-response, or students giving answers they think are expected.

items.stem: Explain why a survey question such as "Don't you agree that the new park is a waste of money?" reduces the validity of the results.
items.answer: It is a leading question that pushes respondents towards one answer, so responses reflect the wording rather than true opinions – the survey does not measure what it intends to.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It is a leading question that pushes respondents towards one answer, so responses reflect the wording rather than true opinions – the survey does not measure what it intends to. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A psychologist designs a reading-speed test. 10 volunteers take it twice, one month apart; their scores (first, second) are: (58, 56); (81, 84); (89, 87); (62, 64); (61, 59); (54, 54); (84, 81); (89, 90); (48, 50); (56, 57). (a) Calculate Pearson's r. (b) Comment on the reliability of the test. (c) Suggest a way to assess the validity of the test. (d) Explain one reason why a high value of r does not, on its own, show that the test is useful.
items.answer: (a) r = 0.991 (b) strong positive correlation (c) criterion-related or content validity (d) consistent but may measure the wrong thing
items.markingKey: (a) M1 A1. (b) R1 strong positive ⇒ reliable. (c) R1 compare with an established measure (criterion) or have experts check content. (d) R1 reliability ≠ validity; small sample of 10.
